reference_title: EM 1110-1-1905, Geotechnical Design of Shallow Foundations on Soils (USACE, 31 July 2025)

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: [p. 246] Problematic ground conditions often require modification to allow acceptable performance of shallow foundations in lieu of more expensive deep foundations; and in some instances, to facilitate excavation for foundation construction (such as ground thawing, dewatering). The application of an improvement technique depends on the ground conditions encountered and other project constraints. Some common ground improvement techniques are presented in this chapter. In some cases, the degree of improvement can be difficult or impossible to fully assess.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-1, printed p. 246.

sections.title: Design requirements
sections.body: [p. 246] Ground improvement designs should be approved by the geotechnical engineer and include the parameters requiring improvement, methods considered for ground improvement, and the rationale for the method selected. Ground improvements can be designed to be either temporary or permanent. Design documents should indicate the proposed equipment, procedural details, quality control measures, method of evaluation, and quality acceptance criteria.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-2, printed p. 246.

sections.title: Improvement methods
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-3, printed p. 246.

sections.title: General
sections.body: [p. 246] General. Table 11-1 summarizes commonly used ground improvement methods, the type of treatment applied, soil suitability, engineering function, and some advantages and limitations of each method. Depending on the ground conditions encountered or other project constraints, ground improvement methods may need to be combined to achieve the project goals. In the following sections, more details are provided for methods applicable to shallow foundations, including applicability, implementation, design issues, and performance evaluation.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-3a, printed p. 246.

sections.title: Improvement alternatives
sections.body: [p. 246] Improvement alternatives. Where problematic ground is encountered, design alternatives that should be considered include: (1) removal and replacement, (2) structure relocation, (3) foundation redesign to meet site constraints, and (4) ground modification (or ground improvement). In some situations, ground improvement methods should be excluded due to design constraints or combined to provide a more reasonable and cost-effective design. Where removal and replacement is selected, dewatering may be necessary. In addition, environmental testing and other controls may be required where uncontrolled fills or environmental contaminants are identified.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-3b, printed p. 246.

sections.title: Evaluation and acceptance
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-4, printed p. 246.

sections.title: Quality assurance
sections.body: [p. 246] Quality assurance. Field monitoring and quality assurance/quality control procedures should be implemented for successful installation of ground improvement projects.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-4a, printed p. 246.

sections.title: Acceptance criteria
sections.body:
[p. 247] Acceptance criteria. Ground improvement techniques have evolved mainly from contractor-led experience and have generally preceded development of engineering guidelines or theoretical treatment. For certain techniques, design methodologies are entirely proprietary and could require performance-based requirements for acceptance. Acceptance criteria should be clearly identified in the contract documents. For certain ground conditions, the degree of improvement can be difficult or impractical to fully quantify (such as karst, uncontrolled fill). Performance evaluation of ground improvement methods is not covered in this manual.

Table 11-1 Ground improvement categories and methods
Category | Function | Method
Densification | Increase soil density, bearing capacity, and reduce settlement. Increases resistance to liquefaction. | 1) Vibro-compaction 2) Stone columns 3) Dynamic compaction 4) Dynamic replacement 5) Compaction grouting 6) Hydro-compaction
Consolidation | Surcharge or preloads applied to decrease settlement. Wick drains can accelerate drainage (settlement). | 1) Preloading/surcharging 2) Drainage
Reinforcement | Increase in shear strength for foundation support, decreases soil compressibility. | 1) Reinforced soil foundation 2) Cohesionless trenches
Chemical stabilization | Increases shear strength and overall bearing capacity. Reduction of shrink/swell potential in certain applications. | 1) Cement/lime mixing 2) Cement grouting 3) Chemical grouting 4) Jet grouting 5) Deep mixing methods
Thermal stabilization | Strength increase. | 1) Lime columns 2) Heating 3) Freezing 4) Active and passive measures
Load reduction | Reduction of load on foundation and corresponding settlement. | 1) Lightweight fill
Expansive soil mitigation | Reduce water infiltration and swell potential of expansive soils. | 1) Moisture barriers 2) Pre-wetting
tables: Table 11-1: Ground improvement categories and methods

sections.title: Densification
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-5, printed p. 248.

sections.title: Vibro-compaction
sections.body:
[p. 248] Vibro-compaction. Vibro-compaction (also known as vibro-floatation) uses vibratory techniques to densify the soil, mainly by the inserting vibrating probes into the ground (Figure 11-1). The initial soil structure is broken down and the soil particles are moved to new packing arrangements using impact and vibration. In saturated cohesionless materials, micro-liquefaction is induced in the process. Densification of the in situ soil occurs rapidly. Ground improvement depths of 60 ft are routinely achieved by vibro-compaction. Depths of 100 ft or more have been attained in some cases.

Figure 11-1. Vibro-compaction, penetration, compaction, backfilling (theengineeringcommunity.org)
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-5a, printed p. 248.

sections.title: Applicability
sections.body:
[p. 248] Applicability. Vibro-compaction is best suited for densification of cohesionless soils with non-plastic fines (passing No. 200 sieve) generally not exceeding 10 percent (Figure 11-2).

Figure 11-2. Suitable soils for vibro-compaction and vibro-replacement methods (McCabe et al. 2007)
figures: Figure 11-2: Suitable soils for vibro-compaction and vibro-replacement methods (McCabe et al. 2007)
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-5a(1), printed p. 248.

sections.title: Implementation
sections.body: [p. 249] Implementation. Vibro-flot™, Terra probe™, vibro-rod, vibro-wing™, and vibrating I-beam are among the common equipment used in vibro compaction. Depending on the type of equipment employed, vibrating frequencies of greater than 30 Hz can be used; the vibration can be applied vertically, horizontally or in both directions. Compaction can be accomplished with or without the addition of cohesionless material (vibro-replacement), and with or without a water jet or compressed air which are applied at the tip of the probe to facilitate its penetration to greater depths and through hard zones. Upward-directed water jets along the sides of the probe have also been helpful.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-5a(2), printed p. 249.

sections.title: Design issues
sections.body: [p. 249] Design issues. Selection of probe pattern, spacing, and depth are required. These parameters depend on the type of soil, the foundation geometry, the required densification, and the equipment used. Triangular, rectangular, and square patterns can be used, and typical spacings are on the order of 3 to 7 ft. For preliminary design, Mitchell (1981) can be used.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-5a(3), printed p. 249.

sections.title: Stone and concrete columns
sections.body: [p. 249] Stone and concrete columns. Stone and concrete columns are constructed using the same equipment and procedure as vibro-compaction, and therefore, are discussed in sequence with vibro-compaction. There are similar products to stone columns, such as compacted aggregate piers, that can be considered for performance and cost-comparison purposes.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-5b, printed p. 249.

sections.title: Applicability
sections.body: [p. 249] Applicability. Both stone and concrete columns are applied to soft cohesive soils and loose sands for the purposes of (1) increasing bearing capacity, (2) reducing settlement and accelerating consolidation, (3) improving slope stability, and (4) mitigating liquefaction. About 10 to 35 percent of the soil mass can be replaced with stone (or sand) in the form of columns, essentially stiffening the soil. Typical column diameters are between 2.5 to 3.5 ft, and the column spacings are typically between 7 and 10 ft. The columns are typically placed in a triangular, square, or hexagonal grid pattern.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-5b(1), printed p. 249.

sections.title: Implementation
sections.body:
[p. 249] Implementation. Stone columns are usually installed either using the dry bottom-feed or the wet, top-feed method. Figure 11-3 illustrates the more common wet, top-feed method of installation. Concreted stone columns are a bottom-feed procedure where a vibratory probe is lowered to the bottom of the hole, then concrete is installed under pressure to form a bulb at the bottom of the hole. The hole is then filled with concrete to the surface. The top-feed procedures involve pushing rock in from the surface. The bottom-feed procedure involves injecting material from the bottom by tremie-like methods.

[p. 250] Figure 11-3. Wet, top-feed installation of stone columns, (a) equipment in position, feed pipe filled, valve open; (b) sinking the vibrator with compressed air (valve closed), and “pull down” assistance; (c) forming the stone column by oscillation; and (d) finishing the stone column
figures: Figure 11-3: Wet, top-feed installation of stone columns, (a) equipment in position, feed pipe filled, valve open; (b) sinking the vibrator with compressed air (valve closed), and “pull down” assistance; (c) forming the stone column by oscillation; and (d) finishing the stone column
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-5b(2), printed pp. 249 to 250.

sections.title: Design issues
sections.body: [p. 250] Design issues. The composite mass of stone columns within the native soil has a lower compressibility and a higher shear strength than those of the native soil alone. The stone columns are stiffer than the soil they replace, however, their stiffness depends on the lateral support by the surrounding soil. If that support is inadequate, the column fails by bulging. The column could also fail as a pile because of insufficient skin friction and end bearing. A larger portion of the applied load can be transferred to the stone columns due to their higher stiffness. This improves the load-carrying capacity of the treated ground and reduces settlement.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-5b(3), printed p. 250.

sections.title: Dynamic compaction
sections.body:
[p. 250] Dynamic compaction. Dynamic compaction is used to increase the allowable bearing capacity and reduce liquefaction potential of the soil. It involves the repeated dropping of large weights by means of crawler cranes on a predetermined grid pattern. The repeated application of the high-energy impacts causes densification of the soil mass to depths ranging from 10 to 30 ft, while some contractors claim densification of 60 ft or more. Figure 11-4 illustrates the dynamic compaction process.

Figure 11-4. Dynamic compaction (Bauer.com)
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-5c, printed p. 250.

sections.title: Applicability
sections.body: [p. 251] Applicability. Dynamic compaction can be used for densification of liquefiable, loose, saturated, cohesionless soils. The use of this method in fine cohesive soils can be uncertain, and therefore, the generation and dissipation of excess pore water pressures should be evaluated. Dynamic compaction should not be used for saturated, fine-grained soils with no additional methods for pore water pressure dissipation. Pore water dissipation in fine-grained soils can be facilitated by the forming drainage channels, by fissuring, or by vertical drains. Another common application can be stabilization of collapsible soils (Rollins and Kim 1994).
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-5c(1), printed p. 251.

sections.title: Implementation
sections.body: [p. 251] Implementation. The weights used in dynamic compaction are usually square or circular in plan but can also be irregularly shaped and quite large in dimension. Drop weights typically consist of concrete blocks, steel plates, or thick steel shells filled with concrete or sand. They normally range from 6 to 35 tons, but heavier weights up to 200 tons have been used. The drop heights usually range from 40 to 80 ft, but heights up to 130 ft have been used. A typical treatment consists of an average of 2 to 3 blows per 10 ft^2 (Mitchell 1981). The drops are made at points spaced many feet apart in a grid pattern. For uniformity and high density in the near-surface zone, surface “ironing” is done by small weight drops over the treated area surface.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-5c(2), printed p. 251.

sections.title: Design issues
sections.body: [p. 251] Design issues.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-5c(3), printed p. 251.

sections.title: Tamper weight, grid pattern, drop heights, and depths of influence are …
sections.body: [p. 251] Tamper weight, grid pattern, drop heights, and depths of influence are calculated during design. A method for determining the depth of influence is provided by FHWA (see FHWA-SA-95-037) and depends on the soil stratification, degree of saturation, and the method of load application. For instance, a free drop is often more efficient than a crane drop. Soft cohesive layers or peat generally dampen the dynamic forces penetrating the soil, and thus the depth of influence is typically reduced.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-5c(3)(a), printed p. 251. The manual prints this subparagraph without a heading; the title is its opening words.

sections.title: FHWA-SA-95-037 (Table 8) presents typical impact energy values per unit volume …
sections.body: [p. 251] FHWA-SA-95-037 (Table 8) presents typical impact energy values per unit volume of treated soils. These values can be multiplied by the thickness of the treated soils to estimate the required applied energy at the surface. The estimated applied energy value can be used to determine the number of drops for a specified spacing or the minimum spacing for a particular number of drops. In addition to determining the energy required to achieve the required densification, the impact of the ground vibrations on adjacent structures should also be evaluated.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-5c(3)(b), printed p. 251. The manual prints this subparagraph without a heading; the title is its opening words.

sections.title: Dynamic replacement
sections.body: [p. 251] Dynamic replacement. Cohesionless inclusions using this improvement method are a form of soil reinforcement. However, because dynamic replacement can be an extension of dynamic compaction, it is discussed in the same sequence. In this method, tamping energy drives cohesionless material down into the craters developed in the compressible soils to form large-diameter soil reinforcement columns (with diameter around 6 to 12 ft). This method combines the advantages from both dynamic compaction and stone columns by creating large-sized inclusions with high internal shear resistance.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-5d, printed p. 251.

sections.title: Applicability
sections.body: [p. 251] Applicability. Dynamic replacement is appliable to cohesionless soils and fills. Dynamic replacement can be formed using a large variety of material. Material [p. 252] recommended is a cohesionless fill material (generally up to 16-inch size), with low fines content (usually less than 15 percent), and free from vegetation or organic matter. The backfill material should be selected for each project depending on local availability. However, successful jobs have been completed with a large variety of material, including demolition debris (such as without wood, metal, and plaster) or crushed, cohesionless backfill material.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-5d(1), printed pp. 251 to 252.

sections.title: Implementation
sections.body:
[p. 252] Implementation. The dynamic replacement process typically usually uses weights with smaller sections as compared to dynamic compaction to improve the penetration and punching of the weight through the soft or loose layer. Through repeated tamping and backfilling phases, dynamic replacement columns are formed by dropping a 10- to 35-ton pounder from heights ranging from 33 to 100 ft. With this technique, replacement ratios of up to 20 to 25 percent can be achieved. Each dynamic replacement column can support loads of up to about 150 tons (Figure 11-5).

Figure 11-5. Dynamic replacement methodology (Ménard Group USA)
figures: Figure 11-5: Dynamic replacement methodology (Ménard Group USA)
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-5d(2), printed p. 252.

sections.title: Design issues
sections.body: [p. 252] Design issues. Dynamic replacement can be adapted to substantial loading conditions (up to 150 tons per column). It is possible to achieve replacement ratios of up to 25 percent. While vibro-stone columns have a limited range of application in organic soft soils (peat and organic clays), dynamic replacement columns can be used in peat or in soils with high organic content without the potential of bulging due to their relatively low slenderness (ratio of height over diameter). Dynamic replacement columns can increase the time rate of consolidation.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-5d(3), printed p. 252.

sections.title: Compaction grouting
sections.body: [p. 252] Compaction grouting. In this displacement grouting method, a stiff grout mixture is injected in the ground to densify loose soil formations. The grout generally does not enter the soil pores. Rather, it remains in a homogeneous mass that displaces and compresses the surrounding soil. Compaction grouting can be used to reduce differential settlements or to provide underpinning and ground strengthening. It can be considered more of a densification method than a chemical stabilization. The system can be used to fill voids.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-5e, printed p. 252.

sections.title: Applicability
sections.body: [p. 253] Applicability. Rubble fills, poorly placed fills, loosened or collapsible soils, soluble rocks, and liquefiable soils.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-5e(1), printed p. 253.

sections.title: Implementation
sections.body:
[p. 253] Implementation. Compaction grouting equipment includes a mixing plant, force-feed piston pumps, hoses, and grout pipes. Compaction-grouted columns (piers) or bulbs are created under foundations to densify the ground and arrest potential ground and structural movements. Single or staggered bulbs are created through vertical or inclined grout pipes (see Figure 11-6). The grout pipes typically have a minimum inside diameter of 50 mm (4 inches) and are flush-jointed to avoid leakage. Soils which are dry of suitable moisture content can be pre-wetted to assist grout take. A recommended ground grout composition is silty sand (10 to 30 percent fines), cement (sometimes with fly ash), additives (such as fluidifiers, accelerators) and water. Coarse aggregates can be used, but they require larger pumps and grout lines.

Figure 11-6. Compaction grouting (a) inclined installation; (b) vertical installation (Geo Grout, gggms.com)
figures: Figure 11-6: Compaction grouting (a) inclined installation; (b) vertical installation (Geo Grout, gggms.com)
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-5e(2), printed p. 253.

sections.title: Design issues
sections.body: [p. 253] Design issues. The design of a compaction grouting involves locating the areas requiring compaction, defining the degree of densification needed, estimating the required grout volume, and selecting grouting layout. The compaction grouting design depends on experience, and a field test could be necessary.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-5e(3), printed p. 253.

sections.title: Hydrocompaction
sections.body: [p. 253] Hydrocompaction. Collapsible soils settle when wetted or vibrated, therefore, the usual approach toward optimizing performance of structures on collapsible soil can be prewetting the construction site.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-5f, printed p. 253.

sections.title: Applicability
sections.body: [p. 253] Applicability. Hydrocompaction is applicable to collapsible soils.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-5f(1), printed p. 253.

sections.title: Implementation
sections.body: [p. 253] Implementation. Ponding or sprinkling water at the surface. Infiltration wells may be used to reach deeper soils.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-5f(2), printed p. 253.

sections.title: Design issues
sections.body: [p. 254] Design issues. When using hydrocompaction, infiltration wells should be used to wet soils to the required depth (Knodel 1992).
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-5f(3), printed p. 254.

sections.title: Consolidation
sections.body: [p. 254] The engineering properties like shear strength and compressibility of a soft cohesive soil improve as the soil consolidates under a sustained static load. This improvement is accompanied by expulsion of water and an associated decrease in volume.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-6, printed p. 254.

sections.title: Preloading/surcharging and drainage
sections.body: [p. 254] Preloading/surcharging and drainage. Preloading, or “surcharging,” is used to protect against unacceptable consolidation settlement. Preloads should exceed the design loads so that the required settlement occurs prior to the construction of the structure or the more permanent fill. Preloading may also be used to shorten the duration needed to achieve primary as well as secondary consolidation. Drainage can be achieved by electro-osmosis. Electro-osmosis is similar to preloading in that effective stresses in the soil are increased and water is removed. The difference is that via electro-osmosis, the water is removed by application of electric potentials over the soil.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-6a, printed p. 254.

sections.title: Prefabricated vertical drains
sections.body: [p. 254] Prefabricated vertical drains. When the anticipated time for compression of the soil under the applied preload is significantly long, prefabricated vertical drains (PVDs) may be installed to accelerate drainage and consolidation settlement as well as increase shear strength. The initial application of vertical drains in the 1920s was to install sand drains. However, the sand drains can collapse during installation and can be costly to install.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-6b, printed p. 254.

sections.title: Applicability
sections.body: [p. 254] Applicability. Soils best suited for consolidation by preloading and electro-osmosis are saturated soft clays, compressible silts, organic silty clays, and peats. The vertical drains are of greatest effectiveness in inorganic clays and silts that exhibit little secondary consolidation.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-6b(1), printed p. 254.

sections.title: Implementation
sections.body: [p. 254] Implementation. Preloading may be accomplished by placing surcharge fills to elevations higher than design. Where necessary, the surcharge fill should be placed in stages to avoid stability failure, with each lift placed only after the soil has gained sufficient strength under the previous lift. For preloading or electro-osmosis, a drainage layer should be constructed to permit water drainage. Electro-osmosis does not involve large volumes of surcharge or stability issues; however, it is more complex in execution than preloading.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-6b(2), printed p. 254.

sections.title: Design issues
sections.body: [p. 254] Design issues. The design of a preloading program involves establishing (1) time-settlement curves under the design load, (2) time-settlement curves under the preload, and (3) evaluation of shear-strength increases under design load at each stage of surcharge. A critical issue with implementation of vertical drains is smear during installation, which can significantly increase the time to reach the required performance objective.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-6b(3), printed p. 254.

sections.title: Reinforcement
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-7, printed p. 255.

sections.title: Reinforced soil foundation
sections.body: [p. 255] Reinforced soil foundation. Geosynthetic-reinforced soil foundations (RSF) act in combination to increase the shear strength of the soil mass, to reduce its settlement under design loads, and to improve its resistance to liquefaction.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-7a, printed p. 255.

sections.title: Applicability
sections.body: [p. 255] Applicability. Reinforcement is applicable to clays, sands, silts, and gravels. Though fine-grained soils are more susceptible to long-term creep deformations, if the intent is to stabilize soils by increasing the confining stress, the reinforcement serves to stabilize the soils during placement and pore water pressure dissipation.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-7a(1), printed p. 255.

sections.title: Implementation
sections.body: [p. 255] Implementation. RSF systems consists of one or more layers of a geosynthetic reinforcement, typically rigid, biaxial geogrids and controlled fill placed below a shallow spread footing to create a composite material with improved performance characteristics (Chen et al. 2007). The presence of reinforcement geosynthetics under the foundation widens the stress bulb, reduces applied stresses to the foundation soils, and works as a stiffened platform or raft.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-7a(2), printed p. 255.

sections.title: Design issues
sections.body:
[p. 255] Design issues. Research has shown that reinforcement produces the most benefit, or the highest bearing capacity ratio (BCR), when the reinforcement layers are within a depth, z equal to one-half of the footing width, B, z = 0.5B (Adams and Collin 1997) (see Figure 11-7). BCR is the bearing capacity of a footing placed on an RSF divided by the bearing capacity of the same footing without reinforcement and can be between 1.5 and 2.0. For a three-layer system, z/B of 0.15, 0.375 and 0.5 found are recommended. The first layer at z/B of 0.15 can be optimal for settlement, s at a level of s/B of 0.5 percent. The RSF should extend 0.5 B past the edge of the footing (each side) with a minimum of 3 ft.

Figure 11-7. Reinforced soil foundation (after Adams and Collin 1997)
figures: Figure 11-7: Reinforced soil foundation (after Adams and Collin 1997)
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-7a(3), printed p. 255.

sections.title: Granular trenches
sections.body:
[p. 255] Granular trenches. To increase the allowable load-bearing capacity and reduce settlement, strip foundations can be constructed over granular trenches neatly excavated in soft clays, as shown in Figure 11-8.

[p. 256] Figure 11-8. Strip footing in soft ground, stabilized with cohesionless trench (after Das 2017)
figures: Figure 11-8: Strip footing in soft ground, stabilized with cohesionless trench (after Das 2017)
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-7b, printed pp. 255 to 256.

sections.title: Applicability
sections.body: [p. 256] Applicability. Granular trenches can be used to improve the load-bearing capacity of strip footings over soft soils.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-7b(1), printed p. 256.

sections.title: Implementation
sections.body: [p. 256] Implementation. Granular trenches in soft soil can be excavated with conventional equipment and do not require extensive excavation outside of the foundation footprint. Encapsulating the cohesionless trench with a geosynthetic layer can improve the performance of supported footings (Mathai and Unnikrishnan 2015).
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-7b(2), printed p. 256.

sections.title: Design issues
sections.body: [p. 256] Design issues. For a cohesionless trench, the ultimate bearing capacity of a foundation can be computed using methods proposed by Das and Hanna (1988) and Das (1989), or commercially available software that models stress and deformation. Bearing capacity generally increases with depth of granular trench.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-7b(3), printed p. 256.

sections.title: Chemical stabilization
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-8, printed p. 256.

sections.title: Cement/lime mixing/cement grouting/chemical grouting
sections.body: [p. 256] Cement/lime mixing/cement grouting/chemical grouting. Cement, lime, fly ash, asphalt, silicate, and other materials are used to stabilize weak soils. They generally bind the soil particles together resulting in higher strength and lower compressibility.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-8a, printed p. 256.

sections.title: Applicability
sections.body: [p. 256] Applicability. Applicable soils vary by method. Cement can be used for sand and collapsing soils. Lime can be used for swelling clays. Cement grouting can be used for coarse soils (less than 15 percent fines), and chemical grouting can be used for fine sand and medium silt.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-8a(1), printed p. 256.

sections.title: Implementation
sections.body: [p. 256] Implementation. Chemical stabilization media (cement, lime, fly ash, etc.) is added to the soil. For clays, the soil dries, making the soil less susceptible to changes in water content (Afrin 2017). When at depth, the chemicals can be applied by injection or by deep mixing methods (DMM).
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-8a(2), printed p. 256.

sections.title: Design issues
sections.body: [p. 256] Design issues. Organic matter, sulphates, sulfides, and carbon dioxide may adversely affect chemical stabilization. Sufficient moisture content must be present. For example, fully hydrated cement requires 20 percent of its own weight of water from the [p. 257] surroundings, and Quicklime can take up to 32 percent of its own weight of water from the surroundings. The pozzolanic reaction is slower with lower temperatures. In cold regions, the soil should be stabilized during the warm season (Afrin 2017).
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-8a(3), printed pp. 256 to 257.

sections.title: Jet grouting
sections.body:
[p. 257] Jet grouting. This technique uses high-pressure fluids applied through a nozzle at the base of a drill pipe to erode the soil particles and mix them with cement grout as the drill bit is rotated and withdrawn, forming hard, impervious columns. Excess soil cuttings are carried to the surface in the form of a waste slurry. The grouted columns can be formed vertically, horizontally, or at an angle. A row of overlapping columns forms a wall (see Figure 11-9).

Figure 11-9. Jet grouting (Geo Grout, gggms.com)
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-8b, printed p. 257.

sections.title: Applicability
sections.body: [p. 257] Applicability. Jet grouting works in most soils since the initial soil structure is broken down and replaced with a composite mass of soil and grout, sometimes called “soilcrete.”
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-8b(1), printed p. 257.

sections.title: Implementation
sections.body: [p. 257] Implementation. Single-, double-, or triple-fluid jet grouting systems are generally used. In the single-fluid system, the fluid can be the grout. The jet simultaneously erodes and binds the soil particles. In the double-fluid system, a second fluid can be used in addition to the grout to enhance the cutting ability of the system. The second fluid can be either compressed air or water. In the triple- fluid system, both air and water are used. The column diameter increases in size from the single- to the triple-fluid system. Horizontal jet grouting uses only the first system. The jet-grouting plant includes a pump, a mixer, a compressed air source, and a water source. A minimum overlapping of 1 ft can be used for rows.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-8b(2), printed p. 257.

sections.title: Design issues
sections.body: [p. 258] Design issues. The design of a jet-grouted column involves the determination of the column diameter, strength, and permeability that would satisfy the project’s requirements. Both the strength and the permeability of the grouted mass are influenced by the cement content in the grout mix. Plots relating strength to cement content are presented by Gallavresi (1992). These plots can be used in the design of the grout mix. The diameter of the constructed column is a function of operating parameters such as injection pressure, grout flow, and rod withdrawal and rotation rates. The slower the withdrawal and rotation rates, the larger the column diameter.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-8b(3), printed p. 258.

sections.title: Deep mixing method
sections.body: [p. 258] Deep mixing method. The DMM technique consists of mixing in-place soils with cement grout or other reagent slurries. Arranging the columns in various configurations permits strengthening of soft soils or for groundwater or liquefaction control.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-8c, printed p. 258.

sections.title: Applicability
sections.body: [p. 258] Applicability. DMM is applicable in soft to stiff silts and clays, sands, and gravels. In extremely dense soils, holes are predrilled using a powerful single-shaft auger to loosen up the ground along the DMM alignment. The obstructions in the soil are removed, if possible, and replaced with good quality fill prior to soil mixing. Although DMM and jet grouting have the same applications, there are two basic differences. Unlike jet grouting, which uses high pressure, high pressure is not used in DMM. In addition, the DMM columns are built to defined dimensions, while jet grouting dimensions are not as clearly defined.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-8c(1), printed p. 258.

sections.title: Implementation
sections.body: [p. 258] Implementation. Hollow-stem, multiple augers with mixing paddles penetrate the ground to the required depth. During penetration and withdrawal, cement grout can be pumped through the auger stem. The auger flights and mixing paddles mix the soil and the grout in place to form continuous, overlapping, soil-cement columns. If needed, steel reinforcement can be inserted in the column to provide bending resistance. A separate pump supplies the grout from the mixing plant to each of the injecting augers. A computer can be used to control grout mixing and flow.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-8c(2), printed p. 258.

sections.title: Design issues
sections.body:
[p. 258] Design issues. The DMM design is influenced by the planned function of the system. When DMM is used for liquefaction control, the DMM can be performed in a block or lattice pattern to resist the stress from foundation or surcharge loadings when loose cohesionless soils liquefy during seismic ground shaking (Figure 11-10). For cut-off-wall construction, DMM can be designed to provide a required permeability. For excavation support, DMM usually has reinforcing members designed to resist bending moments and shear stress along the wall.

[p. 259] Figure 11-10. Deep mixing method for liquefaction control (Taki and Yang 1991)
figures: Figure 11-10: Deep mixing method for liquefaction control (Taki and Yang 1991)
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-8c(3), printed pp. 258 to 259.

sections.title: Thermal stabilization
sections.body: [p. 259] Heating of soils can reduce the water content and reduce the shrink-swell potential for expansive clays. Freezing of soils can also stabilize soils. In areas of permafrost, settlement can be significantly reduced by freezing existing soils that are subject to thawing. To protect soils from temperature variation in cold areas, the soil can be graded to reduce exposure of the soil to temperature variations, air convection can be used, or a heat drain can be installed (Doré et al. 2012).
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-9, printed p. 259.

sections.title: Applicability
sections.body: [p. 259] Applicability. Thermal stabilization is applicable to expansive clays. Freezing is applicable to soils that are frozen for much of the year.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-9a, printed p. 259.

sections.title: Implementation
sections.body: [p. 259] Implementation. There has been some advancement in ground freezing (Bayasan et al. 2008). Insulation is another option. For some applications, the soil can be frozen with pipes, refrigerants, and chillers.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-9b, printed p. 259.

sections.title: Design issues
sections.body: [p. 259] Design issues. Heating can result in permanent changes to the soil properties, which turns expansive clays into non-plastic materials. Similarly, freezing can reduce settlement of existing foundations built on permafrost. In other applications, freezing will turn very soft materials into hard materials. Heating and freezing methods can be costly and energy intensive. For freezing methods, property changes remain only when the soil is frozen. Like seepage or consolidation analyses, a thermal analysis can be performed. Thermal conductivity, latent heat of fusion, heat of vaporization of soil water, and heat capacity of soil are needed for analysis.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-9c, printed p. 259.

sections.title: Load reduction
sections.body: [p. 259] Certain soil, rock, concrete, and man-made materials can be used to reduce settlement and can increase stability of foundation soils. The amount of settlement reduction is directly proportional to the reduction in load. Shear strength properties vary depending on the material selected.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-10, printed p. 259.

sections.title: Applicability
sections.body: [p. 260] Applicability. Lightweight fill is generally used above or as a replacement to soft and compressible natural soil.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-10a, printed p. 260.

sections.title: Implementation
sections.body: [p. 260] Implementation. Lightweight fills are usually obtained from a controlled source (such as manufactured, processed) and can require proprietary placement methods.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-10b, printed p. 260.

sections.title: Design issues
sections.body: [p. 260] Design issues. Granular lightweight fills typically have a shear strength like natural soils, while cemented fills and man-made products are generally characterized by compressive strength. Lightweight fill density can vary from about 1 to 65 pcf depending on the type selected.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-10c, printed p. 260.

sections.title: Expansive soil mitigation
sections.body: [p. 260] Removal of surface swell potential soils and replacement with non-expansive or low-expansive, low-permeable backfill can reduce heave at the ground surface and should be used in conjunction with surface drainage controls (such as directing drainage away from foundations). Lime modification can also be used to reduce volume changes and to increase the strength of foundation soils.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-11, printed p. 260.

sections.title: Applicability
sections.body: [p. 260] Applicability. Controlled backfill, lime modification, and drainage controls are used to reduce heave potential of expansive soils.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-11a, printed p. 260.

sections.title: Implementation
sections.body: [p. 260] Implementation. Typically, 4 to 8 ft of surface expansive soils are removed and replaced with compacted soils that have a low degree of heave potential. Lime modification requires mixing lime with the natural soils and can typically be achieved over a depth of several feet.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-11b, printed p. 260.

sections.title: Design issues
sections.body: [p. 260] Design issues. Controlled backfills (such as low-permeability soils with low heave potential) could be difficult to source. Where lime modification is used, excavation and replacement below foundations may be required where low-volume change material fill heights are insufficient to reduce heave potential to within tolerable levels.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 11 (Ground Improvement), paragraph 11-11c, printed p. 260.
